situation:
You are to assume the role of race information manager at STONE CREEK ENDURANCE, a running and endurance event series owned by the people who work in it. The member-elected operations director (judge) has asked you to recommend how the next half marathon should be staffed at the points where the crowd builds, and to be ready to explain your reasoning.

At the last race, spectators pushed past a barricade near the finish and two people were treated for minor injuries. Since then the co-op has pulled together what it already holds: entry gate counts, timing mat splits, and location pings from the race app that runners and spectators both carry. Together those records describe where people actually stood, minute by minute, along the closed roads.

That record points away from the finish chute. Crowd density peaked at the second-to-last corner, where the course narrows between a park wall and a row of vendor tents, and it stayed high there for eleven minutes before the barricade gave way farther on. Moving four marshals from the chute to that corner is what the record supports, and it costs the co-op nothing to do.

Those marshals are member-owners who have worked this course for nine years, and they say the chute is where it always goes wrong. Redeploying them thins the chute on the one stretch the crew trusts least and asks the crew to accept a reading it cannot check itself. Keeping them in the chute and hiring eight more marshals for the corner instead spends money the members voted to hold for the next race's medical tent.

The operations director (judge) wants your recommendation on where the marshals stand, on what the co-op should do with the information it now collects about its own events, and on what it costs to keep collecting it. The operations director (judge) will greet you, ask to hear your ideas, and will thank you after your presentation and questions.
